title: Pharaoh, the Monster of the Nile
summary: God declares himself against Pharaoh, pictured as a great monster lying in the Nile who claims to have made the river himself. He will be hauled out with hooks and left in the desert, and Egypt, a splintered reed that wounded Israel when it leaned on it, will be desolate for forty years and then restored as a lowly kingdom. A later oracle, the latest dated in the book, gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as wages for his unrewarded siege of Tyre, and promises a horn for Israel.
story: Chapters 29 to 32 are the last and longest block of the oracles against the nations, seven oracles against Egypt, six of them dated. Egypt receives more attention than any other nation because it was the power Judah's kings kept trusting instead of God. Zedekiah's rebellion against Babylon was built on the hope of Egyptian help, and that hope had failed. The chapter answers the question of Egypt's future: it will not be destroyed forever, but it will never again be a great power that Israel can rely on. Verse 21, with its promise of a horn for Israel and an opened mouth for the prophet, looks ahead to the restoration and to the moment in chapter 33 when Ezekiel's long silence ends.
historical:
The first oracle is dated to the tenth year, tenth month, twelfth day, in January 587 BC, about a year into the siege of Jerusalem. The Pharaoh at the time was Hophra, known to Greek writers as Apries, who reigned from about 589 to 570 BC and is named in Jeremiah 44:30. Jeremiah records that an Egyptian army marched out during the siege and the Babylonians briefly withdrew from Jerusalem, only to return when the Egyptians went home (Jeremiah 37:5-11). That episode is probably the splintered reed of verses 6 and 7. The same image had been used over a century earlier by the Assyrian official who taunted Hezekiah for trusting Egypt, a staff of crushed reed that pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it (2 Kings 18:21).

Verses 17 to 21 are dated to the twenty-seventh year, first month, first day, in the spring of 571 BC, the latest date in the book. By then Nebuchadnezzar's long siege of Tyre had ended without the plunder his army expected. A fragmentary Babylonian text appears to record a campaign by Nebuchadnezzar against Egypt in his thirty-seventh year, about 568 or 567 BC, during the reign of Hophra's successor Amasis, though its details are uncertain. Migdol to Syene (verse 10) means from the northern frontier to Aswan in the far south; Pathros is Upper Egypt, and Cush lay beyond it to the south, in what is now Sudan.
cultural:
The Nile was Egypt's life. Almost no rain fell, and the whole country depended on the river's annual flood. Pharaoh was regarded as a divine king who guaranteed the order of the world, including the river's flow. Pharaoh's boast in verse 3, The Nile is mine; I made it myself, expresses that ideology, and God's reply mocks it. The great monster (tannin) is probably the crocodile, a feared creature of the Nile and associated in Egypt with divine power, but the word is also used in the Old Testament for the sea dragon of chaos (Isaiah 27:1; 51:9). The picture of hooking a crocodile recalls Job 41:1-2, where God asks Job whether he can draw out Leviathan with a hook.

Leaving a body unburied in the open field to be eaten by birds and beasts (verse 5) was a horror in every ancient culture, and especially in Egypt, where elaborate burial was central to religion. For Pharaoh, whose tomb was meant to secure his eternal life, it was the worst fate imaginable.
literary: The chapter contains two dated oracles. The first (verses 1 to 16) combines a mythic picture, the monster hauled out of the river, with a historical charge, Egypt's betrayal of Israel as a broken reed, and ends with a prophecy of restoration to a humbled state. Its structure moves in three steps, each with the recognition formula they will know that I am the LORD (verses 6, 9, and 16). The second oracle (verses 17 to 21) is a startling appendix, placed here by subject rather than by date. It openly revises the expectations of chapter 26, admitting that Nebuchadnezzar received no wages from Tyre and assigning Egypt to him instead. The book's willingness to keep both oracles side by side is itself worth noticing.

outline.t: Pharaoh the monster hauled from the Nile
Restored as the lowliest of kingdoms
Egypt given to Nebuchadnezzar as wages for Tyre
A horn for Israel and an opened mouth

doctrines.note: Pharaoh claims to have made the Nile, taking to himself the glory of the Creator. Israel's reliance on Egypt was a related idolatry: trusting a proud human power in place of God.
God assigns Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as wages for work done for him (verse 20). Even a pagan king's campaigns are counted as service within God's purposes.
Egypt is judged but not wiped out; after forty years it is gathered again, though humbled. And for Israel, God promises to cause a horn to sprout (verse 21), a sign of renewed strength.

words.note: Tannin, a great monster, serpent, or dragon. It can mean a large reptile such as a crocodile, or the chaos monster of the sea that God subdues in poetic texts. Pharaoh is portrayed as both, a creature of the Nile and a power of chaos, and God hauls him out like a fish.

Mish'enet, a staff or support, something to lean on. Egypt was supposed to be Israel's support against Babylon, but it proved a staff of reed that splintered in the hand. The image exposes the folly of trusting in human power.
Qeren, horn, a common biblical symbol of strength, drawn from the horns of an animal. To cause a horn to sprout is to renew power and dignity. Psalm 132:17 uses the same image for the line of David.
Pe'ullah, wages or recompense for labor. Nebuchadnezzar's army worked hard against Tyre and was not paid; God pays them with Egypt. The word frames the Babylonian king as a laborer hired by God.

christ: Verse 21 promises that God will cause a horn to sprout for the house of Israel. The image of a sprouting horn is used in Psalm 132:17 for the royal line of David, and in Luke's Gospel Zechariah praises God for raising up a horn of salvation in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69), speaking of the coming of Jesus. Ezekiel's own words may simply mean a renewal of Israel's strength, but they belong to the stream of hope that the New Testament sees fulfilled in the son of David. The chapter's picture of Pharaoh, who claimed to have made the river, also sets up a contrast that runs through the Bible: the true King is the Creator who made the world, and in the New Testament the Word through whom all things were made becomes flesh not to boast but to serve (John 1:3, 14).

hard.q: Was Egypt ever desolate for forty years, as verses 11 to 13 say?
hard.a: There is no known period in which Egypt lay uninhabited for forty years, and readers who take the Bible seriously have answered in more than one way. Many interpreters understand forty years as a round, symbolic number, a generation of punishment like Israel's forty years in the wilderness and the forty years of Judah's guilt in Ezekiel 4:6. On this reading the point is that Egypt, like Israel, would suffer a period of judgment and then be restored in a diminished state. Others point to Babylonian and later Persian invasions of Egypt and to the deportation of Egyptians, and see a looser fulfillment in Egypt's loss of power and independence. The most secure part of the prophecy is its conclusion: Egypt did cease to be a great imperial power in the Near East, and after the Persian conquest in 525 BC it was ruled by foreign dynasties, Persian, Greek, and Roman, for most of the following centuries. The chapter's focus is less on predicting a precise timeline than on Egypt's future as a lowly kingdom that Israel would never again trust.

questions: Pharaoh said, The Nile is mine; I made it myself. What gifts do you treat as your own achievement rather than God's provision?
Egypt was a reed that splintered when Israel leaned on it. What have you leaned on that turned out to wound you?
Ezekiel's book kept both the oracle against Tyre and the later admission that it had not been fulfilled as expected. What does that honesty teach about how to read prophecy?
